summary: Teach natural selection as a four-ingredient mechanism — variation, heritability, competition/over-reproduction, and differential survival & reproduction — that shifts the FREQUENCY of a trait across a population over generations, while no individual changes its own inherited trait to fit the environment. Learners should assemble these conditions into a causal chain, apply them to a data-rich case (peppered moth, antibiotic resistance), explain why advantaged individuals leave more offspring, and distinguish the mechanism (selection: differential survival and reproduction) from the result (evolution: change in heritable trait/allele frequency across generations, which can build into large change over many generations). The load-bearing correction is anti-Lamarckian: the environment filters pre-existing heritable variation; it does not let organisms acquire and pass on traits they 'need'. Activities span a runnable population model, articulation/sorting tasks, Socratic challenge of lifetime-adaptation language, and vocabulary pre-teaching, each with a stated affordance and limit.
misconceptions: Believing individuals change/adapt themselves to suit the environment during their lifetime and pass on those acquired changes (Lamarckism).
Thinking organisms mutate or develop traits 'because they need them' — need-driven, directed change rather than selection of pre-existing variation.
Treating natural selection as acting on individuals rather than shifting trait frequencies across a POPULATION over generations.
Reading 'survival of the fittest' as 'the strongest/biggest survive' rather than 'those best suited to the environment leave the most offspring'.
Conflating natural selection (mechanism) with evolution (the long-term result), or thinking evolution has a goal/progress toward 'better' organisms.
Assuming selection creates new traits, rather than filtering variation that already exists in the population.

activities.title: Run the generations: watch the population shift while individuals stay fixed
steps: Look down on a population of pale-and-dark moths resting on pale lichen-covered bark, alongside a live histogram of their shades.
Flip one lever so industrial soot darkens the bark, then press 'run a generation' and watch a bird predator pick off more of the now-conspicuous pale moths than dark ones before they breed.
Observe the darker survivors (variants that already existed) reproduce and pass the darker shade to offspring, and watch the histogram slide from pale-dominated to dark-dominated across generations.

Confirm the key dissociation: track any single moth and verify it never darkened itself — individuals keep the shade they were born with for life; the population changed only because survivors were the ones that bred.
Scrub the soot away and run more generations to see the population march back toward pale, tracking the environment.

Start a fresh run in which no dark variant exists at all and watch the population fail to adapt — with no favourable variant to select, it declines (in this model, toward extinction) — showing selection can only filter variation already present, never conjure a trait a moth 'needs'.
Read off the data readout to build an evidence-based explanation of why the trait frequency changed.
activities.insight: Natural selection is a population-level, statistical process over generations: unchanging individuals plus differential survival and reproduction of pre-existing heritable variants produce a shifting trait frequency. Individuals do not adapt themselves; the population changes because survivors reproduce, and selection can only act on variation that is already there.

activities.title: Assemble and sort: the four conditions and correct-vs-Lamarckian accounts
steps: Order the four conditions into the causal chain: variation → heritability → competition/over-reproduction → differential survival & reproduction → frequency change.
Given an account of antibiotic resistance, choose the correct population-level explanation over an incorrect Lamarckian alternative (e.g. 'the bacteria tried to become resistant').
Sort a set of statements about a case into 'correct natural-selection account' versus 'organism chose/needed to adapt'.

From before/after population descriptions, identify the mechanism (which pre-existing variants survived and reproduced more) and the result (the change in heritable trait frequency in later generations), noting that even a one-generation shift in heritable trait frequency is evolution, while large changes build up over many generations.
activities.insight: The four conditions form a checklist that applies to any example, and correct accounts reason at the population level and distinguish mechanism from result; Lamarckian and need-driven phrasings can be identified and rejected.

activities.title: Explain it to a sceptical biologist (Socratic challenge)
steps: Take on a case with an in-role evolutionary biologist (or Darwin) who asks the learner to explain how a population became resistant or camouflaged.
Respond to pushback whenever lifetime-adaptation or need-driven language slips in (e.g. 'the moth changed to survive', 'they needed longer necks').
Rebuild the account toward pre-existing variation plus differential reproduction, naming each of the four conditions in the case.

Answer probing questions such as: where did the first longer-necked giraffes come from before any selection happened? Did the bacteria try to become resistant? What is the difference here between natural selection and evolution?
activities.insight: Articulating the mechanism aloud and defending it against challenge helps a learner catch and replace their own Lamarckian or teleological phrasing with population-level, variation-plus-differential-reproduction reasoning.

activities.title: Pre-teach the vocabulary with a labelled peppered-moth case
steps: Explore a labelled peppered-moth before/after image where each of the four conditions can be revealed with its role in the case.
Answer a lift-the-flap prompt: 'did the moths change, or did the population?'
Match each condition term (variation, heritability, competition, differential survival) to its meaning in the moth example before moving to the runnable model.
activities.insight: Learners gain the vocabulary and a labelled outcome of a classic case, building readiness to reason about the process itself.

checkQuestion: Giraffes have long necks. A student explains: 'Over their lives, giraffes kept stretching to reach high leaves, their necks got longer, and they passed those longer necks to their babies — that's how the species got long necks.' Is that the right explanation? Give the natural-selection account instead.
checkAnswer: No — that's the Lamarckian stretching story. In the population there was already heritable variation in neck length; giraffes with longer necks could reach more food, so they survived and reproduced more, passing on the long-neck alleles. Over many generations the average neck length increased. Individuals don't stretch and pass on the result; the population changes because some variants leave more offspring.
